name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MATCH_Q01 - Organisms and their genomic DNA lengths

questiontext.text:
Match the organisms in the left column with their characteristic DNA lengths in the right column, and select the correct combination.

OrganismDNA Length
A. Bacteriophage \(\phi \times 174\)i. \(48502\text{ bp}\)
B. Bacteriophage lambdaii. \(3.3 \times 10^9\text{ bp}\)
C. Escherichia coliiii. \(5386\text{ nucleotides}\)
D. Human (haploid content)iv. \(4.6 \times 10^6\text{ bp}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The length of DNA is a characteristic feature of an organism and is defined either as the number of nucleotides (for single-stranded DNA) or as the number of base pairs (for double-stranded DNA).

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Organism
Bacteriophage \(\phi \times 174\) has single-stranded DNA consisting of \(5386\text{ nucleotides}\). Bacteriophage lambda has a genome size of \(48502\text{ bp}\). The bacterium Escherichia coli possesses \(4.6 \times 10^6\text{ bp}\), while the haploid content of human DNA is \(3.3 \times 10^9\text{ bp}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Bacteriophage \(\phi \times 174\) with \(5386\text{ nucleotides}\), Bacteriophage lambda with \(48502\text{ bp}\), Escherichia coli with \(4.6 \times 10^6\text{ bp}\), and Human (haploid content) with \(3.3 \times 10^9\text{ bp}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MATCH_Q02 - Scientists and landmark molecular biology discoveries

questiontext.text:
Match the scientists with their landmark contributions to molecular genetics, and choose the correct combination.

Scientist(s)Contribution
A. Friedrich Meischeri. Proved DNA is the genetic material using bacteriophages
B. Frederick Griffithii. First identified DNA as an acidic substance named 'Nuclein'
C. Hershey and Chaseiii. Developed DNA fingerprinting using VNTR probes
D. Alec Jeffreysiv. Discovered the transforming principle in Streptococcus pneumoniae

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The identification and characterisation of DNA as the genetic material and its forensic applications resulted from key historical experiments.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Contribution
Friedrich Meischer (1869) first identified DNA as an acidic substance in the nucleus and named it 'Nuclein'. Frederick Griffith (1928) observed transformation of rough non-virulent Streptococcus pneumoniae into smooth virulent bacteria via a 'transforming principle'. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase (1952) provided unequivocal proof that DNA is the genetic material using radiolabelled bacteriophages. Alec Jeffreys initially developed the technique of DNA fingerprinting using Variable Number of Tandem Repeats (VNTR) as a probe.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Friedrich Meischer with 'Nuclein', Frederick Griffith with the transforming principle, Hershey and Chase with bacteriophage proof of DNA as genetic material, and Alec Jeffreys with DNA fingerprinting.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MATCH_Q03 - Eukaryotic RNA polymerases and transcription factors

questiontext.text:
Match the enzymes and transcription factors with their specific roles in transcription, and select the correct option.

Enzyme / FactorRole in Transcription
A. RNA polymerase Ii. Transcribes heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA)
B. RNA polymerase IIii. Transcribes tRNA, \(5\text{S rRNA}\), and snRNAs
C. RNA polymerase IIIiii. Facilitates termination of bacterial transcription
D. Rho (\(\rho\)) factoriv. Transcribes \(28\text{S}\), \(18\text{S}\), and \(5.8\text{S}\) rRNAs

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In eukaryotes, three nuclear RNA polymerases exhibit a clear division of labour, whereas in bacteria a single RNA polymerase associates transiently with initiation (\(\sigma\)) and termination (\(\rho\)) factors.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Enzyme and Factor
RNA polymerase I transcribes ribosomal RNAs (\(28\text{S}\), \(18\text{S}\), and \(5.8\text{S}\)). RNA polymerase II transcribes the precursor of mRNA, known as heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA). RNA polymerase III is responsible for transcribing tRNA, \(5\text{S rRNA}\), and small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs). In bacteria, the Rho (\(\rho\)) factor associates with RNA polymerase to terminate transcription.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: RNA polymerase I with \(28\text{S}, 18\text{S}, 5.8\text{S}\) rRNAs; RNA polymerase II with hnRNA; RNA polymerase III with tRNA, \(5\text{S rRNA}\), and snRNAs; and Rho factor with bacterial transcription termination.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MATCH_Q04 - Regulatory and structural genes of lac operon

questiontext.text:
Match the genes of the lac operon with their respective protein products, and select the correct combination.

GeneProduct
A. \(i\) genei. \(\beta\)-galactosidase
B. \(z\) geneii. Transacetylase
C. \(y\) geneiii. Repressor protein
D. \(a\) geneiv. Permease

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The lac operon in E. coli consists of one regulatory gene (\(i\)) and three polycistronic structural genes (\(z\), \(y\), and \(a\)) involved in lactose metabolism.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Gene
The \(i\) gene (derived from inhibitor) codes for the repressor protein of the lac operon. The \(z\) gene codes for \(\beta\)-galactosidase, which hydrolyses lactose into galactose and glucose. The \(y\) gene codes for permease, which increases cell permeability to \(\beta\)-galactosides. The \(a\) gene encodes transacetylase.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: \(i\) gene with repressor protein, \(z\) gene with \(\beta\)-galactosidase, \(y\) gene with permease, and \(a\) gene with transacetylase.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MATCH_Q05 - Triplet codons and their corresponding amino acids

questiontext.text:
Match the mRNA codons with their corresponding amino acid or translation function, and choose the correct combination.

mRNA CodonAmino Acid / Function
A. AUGi. Stop (terminator) codon
B. UUUii. Methionine and initiator codon
C. UAAiii. Tryptophan
D. UGGiv. Phenylalanine

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The genetic code consists of \(64\) triplet codons, of which \(61\) code for amino acids and \(3\) act as stop codons.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Codon
AUG has dual functions: it codes for Methionine and acts as the initiator codon. UUU codes for Phenylalanine across almost all organisms from bacteria to humans. UAA (along with UAG and UGA) does not code for any amino acid and functions as a stop terminator codon. UGG is the sole codon for Tryptophan.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: AUG with Methionine and initiator codon, UUU with Phenylalanine, UAA with stop codon, and UGG with Tryptophan.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MATCH_Q06 - Chemical linkages in a DNA double helix

questiontext.text:
Match the chemical linkages in a polynucleotide chain and DNA double helix with their correct structural descriptions.

Chemical LinkageStructural Description
A. N-glycosidic linkagei. Links a phosphate group to \(5'\text{C}\) OH of a nucleoside
B. Phosphoester linkageii. Links two nucleotides to form a dinucleotide
C. \(3'-5'\) phosphodiester linkageiii. Pairs complementary bases of opposite strands
D. Hydrogen bondiv. Links a nitrogenous base to \(1'\text{C}\) OH of pentose sugar

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides assembled via specific covalent linkages within each strand and non-covalent hydrogen bonds between complementary strands.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Linkage
A nitrogenous base attaches to the OH of \(1'\text{C}\) of a pentose sugar through an N-glycosidic linkage to form a nucleoside. A phosphate group attaches to the OH of \(5'\text{C}\) of a nucleoside through a phosphoester linkage to form a nucleotide. Two nucleotides are joined through a \(3'-5'\) phosphodiester linkage to form a dinucleotide. Complementary bases on opposite strands are held together by hydrogen bonds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: N-glycosidic linkage with linking base to \(1'\text{C}\) OH of sugar; phosphoester linkage with linking phosphate to \(5'\text{C}\) OH of nucleoside; \(3'-5'\) phosphodiester linkage with linking two nucleotides; and hydrogen bond with pairing complementary bases.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MATCH_Q07 - Contributions to deciphering the genetic code

questiontext.text:
Match the scientists involved in proposing and deciphering the genetic code with their specific contributions.

ScientistContribution
A. George Gamowi. Chemical synthesis of RNA with defined base combinations
B. Har Gobind Khoranaii. Template-independent enzymatic RNA polymerisation
C. Marshall Nirenbergiii. Argued that the genetic code should be a triplet
D. Severo Ochoaiv. Cell-free system for protein synthesis to decipher the code

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Deciphering the genetic code required theoretical reasoning by physicists and experimental breakthroughs in organic chemistry and biochemistry.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Scientist
George Gamow, a physicist, argued that \(4^3 = 64\) combinations of three nucleotides are needed to code for \(20\) amino acids. Har Gobind Khorana developed chemical methods to synthesise RNA molecules with defined base combinations (homopolymers and copolymers). Marshall Nirenberg developed a cell-free system for protein synthesis that finally helped decipher the genetic code. Severo Ochoa's enzyme (polynucleotide phosphorylase) enabled polymerisation of RNA with defined sequences in a template-independent manner.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: George Gamow with the triplet code proposal; Har Gobind Khorana with chemical synthesis of defined RNA; Marshall Nirenberg with the cell-free protein synthesis system; and Severo Ochoa with template-independent enzymatic RNA synthesis.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MATCH_Q08 - Quantitative features of the human genome

questiontext.text:
Match the features of the human genome discovered through the Human Genome Project with their corresponding values.

Human Genome FeatureValue / Description
A. Dystrophini. Fewest genes among human chromosomes (\(231\))
B. Chromosome 1ii. Largest known human gene (\(2.4\) million bases)
C. Chromosome Yiii. Single-base DNA differences at \(\approx 1.4\) million locations
D. SNPsiv. Most genes among human chromosomes (\(2968\))

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Human Genome Project revealed exact gene counts, chromosome-level gene distributions, and single-nucleotide variations across the human genome.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Feature
While the average human gene consists of \(3000\) bases, sizes vary greatly, with dystrophin being the largest known human gene at \(2.4\) million bases. Chromosome 1 has the most genes (\(2968\)), whereas the Y chromosome has the fewest (\(231\)). Scientists have also identified about \(1.4\) million locations where single-base DNA differences, called single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), occur in humans.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Dystrophin with \(2.4\) million bases, Chromosome 1 with \(2968\) genes, Chromosome Y with \(231\) genes, and SNPs with single-base differences at approximately \(1.4\) million locations.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CHAPTER6_MATCH_Q09 - RNA processing and translation mechanisms

questiontext.text:
Match the molecular processes or catalytic components involved in RNA maturation and translation with their correct descriptions.

Process / ComponentDescription
A. Cappingi. Activation of amino acids using ATP and linking to cognate tRNA
B. Tailingii. Ribozyme catalysing peptide bond formation in bacteria
C. Aminoacylation of tRNAiii. Addition of methyl guanosine triphosphate at the \(5'\)-end
D. \(23\text{S rRNA}\)iv. Template-independent addition of \(200\text{–}300\) adenylate residues at \(3'\)-end

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Eukaryotic primary transcripts (hnRNA) undergo post-transcriptional modifications before translation, and translation itself relies on amino acid activation and ribosomal catalysis.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Process and Component
During capping, an unusual nucleotide (methyl guanosine triphosphate) is added to the \(5'\)-end of hnRNA. During tailing, \(200\text{–}300\) adenylate residues are added at the \(3'\)-end in a template-independent manner. Charging of tRNA, or aminoacylation of tRNA, involves activating amino acids in the presence of ATP and linking them to their cognate tRNA. During translation, \(23\text{S rRNA}\) in bacteria acts as a ribozyme (RNA enzyme) to catalyse peptide bond formation.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct pairings are: Capping with addition of methyl guanosine triphosphate at the \(5'\)-end; Tailing with template-independent addition of \(200\text{–}300\) adenylate residues at the \(3'\)-end; Aminoacylation of tRNA with ATP-dependent activation and linking of amino acids to tRNA; and \(23\text{S rRNA}\) with bacterial ribozyme activity.
